gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Sovereign Nature of the Indian State
children: Sovereign meaning India is neither a dependency nor a dominion of any other nation
India as an independent state with no authority above it and freedom to conduct own internal and external affairs
India's full membership of the Commonwealth of Nations in 1949 does not affect sovereignty
British Crown as head of the Commonwealth is an extra-constitutional declaration
India's membership of the United Nations in 1945 constitutes no limitation on sovereignty
India's ability to acquire or cede foreign territory as a sovereign state
India ceased to be a British dominion on January 26, 1950 by declaring herself a sovereign republic
India was a dominion from August 15, 1947 to January 26, 1950
Pakistan continued as a British Dominion until 1956
Pandit Nehru's statement: Commonwealth membership is by free will and can be terminated by free will
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Socialist Character of the Indian State
children: Socialist added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)
Socialist content implicit in Directive Principles before the amendment
Congress party resolution for 'socialistic pattern of society' at Avadi session (1955)
Indian socialism is 'democratic socialism' – faith in a mixed economy where public and private sectors co-exist
Democratic socialism contrasted with communistic socialism (nationalisation and abolition of private property)
Supreme Court (Nakara v. Union of India, 1983): democratic socialism aims to end poverty, ignorance, disease and inequality of opportunity
Indian socialism as a blend of Marxism and Gandhism, leaning towards Gandhian socialism
G.B. Pant University v. State of U.P. (2000) – related to democratic socialism
New Economic Policy (1991) – liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation led to dilution of socialist credentials
Congress resolution also called for social ownership/control and equitable distribution of national wealth
Indira Gandhi statement: own brand of socialism, not just nationalisation
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Secular Character of the Indian State
children: Secular added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)
Supreme Court in 1974: despite no express mention, Constitution-makers wanted a secular state
Articles 25 to 28 guarantee fundamental right to freedom of religion
Indian Constitution's positive concept of secularism: all religions have same status and support from state
Atheistic State (anti-religion) and Theocratic State (pro-religion with state religion) contrasted
Secular State: neutral in matter of religion, no state religion (e.g., USA, India)
H.R. Gokhale's definition of secularism (Union Law Minister)
P.B. Gajendragadkar's definition of secularism (former Chief Justice of India)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Democratic Polity under the Indian Constitution
children: Democratic polity based on doctrine of popular sovereignty
Two types of democracy: direct and indirect
Direct democracy: people exercise supreme power directly (e.g., Switzerland)
Four devices of direct democracy: Referendum, Initiative, Recall, Plebiscite with definitions
Indirect democracy: representatives elected by people exercise supreme power
Representative democracy: two kinds – parliamentary and presidential
Indian Constitution provides for representative parliamentary democracy
Executive responsible to legislature for all policies and actions in parliamentary democracy
Manifestations of democratic character: universal adult franchise, periodic elections, rule of law, independence of judiciary, absence of discrimination
Term 'democratic' embraces political, social and economic democracy
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Republic Nature of the Indian State
children: Republic: head of state elected directly or indirectly for a fixed period
Monarchy contrasted: head of state hereditary (e.g., Britain)
Republic: head of state elected (e.g., USA)
India has an elected head called the President
President elected indirectly for a fixed period of five years
Political sovereignty vests in the people, not a single individual like a king
Absence of any privileged class; all public offices open to every citizen without discrimination
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Justice in the Preamble
children: Justice embracing three forms: social, economic and political
Justice secured through Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
Social justice: equal treatment without social distinction; improvement of conditions of backward classes (SCs, STs, OBCs) and women
Economic justice: non-discrimination based on economic factors; elimination of glaring inequalities in wealth, income and property
Distributive justice: combination of social justice and economic justice
Political justice: equal political rights, equal access to political offices, equal voice in government
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Liberty in the Preamble
children: Liberty: absence of restraints on activities and provision of opportunities for development of individual personalities
Preamble secures liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship through Fundamental Rights
Liberty enforceable in court of law
Liberty essential for successful functioning of Indian democratic system
Liberty does not mean license to do what one likes
Liberty to be enjoyed within limitations mentioned in the Constitution
Liberty conceived as qualified, not absolute
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Equality in the Preamble – General Principles
children: Equality: absence of special privileges; provision of adequate opportunities for all without discrimination
Preamble secures equality of status and opportunity
Three dimensions of equality: civic, political, economic
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Fraternity and National Integration
children: Fraternity: sense of brotherhood
Single citizenship as promoter of fraternity
Fraternity assures dignity of the individual
Fraternity assures unity and integrity of the nation
Word 'integrity' added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)
'Dignity of the individual' signifies material betterment, democratic set-up, and sacredness of individual personality
'Unity and integrity of the nation' – psychological and territorial dimensions of national integration
Indestructible nature of the Indian Union (states have no right to secede)
Hindrances to national integration: communalism, regionalism, casteism, linguism, secessionism
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Status of the Preamble as part of the Constitution (Judicial Decisions)
children: Berubari Union case (1960): Supreme Court opined Preamble is not a part of the Constitution
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): rejected earlier opinion, held Preamble is a part of the Constitution
LIC of India case (1995): reaffirmed Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
Constituent Assembly enacted Preamble after the rest of the Constitution to ensure conformity
Motion adopted that Preamble stands part of the Constitution
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Amenability of the Preamble
children: Preamble can be amended under Article 368
Kesavananda Bharati case: question raised whether Preamble can be amended
Petitioner contended Preamble is not part of Constitution, so cannot be amended
Supreme Court held Preamble can be amended subject to no amendment to the 'basic features'
Basic features in Preamble (e.g., sovereign, democratic, republic, secular, socialist) cannot be altered
Preamble amended only once by 42nd Amendment (1976) – added Socialist, Secular, Integrity
Validity of 42nd Amendment upheld
